notes.text: Arise — This is God's command to Micah. Contend thou - Argue the case between God and thy people; and speak as if thou wouldst make the mountains hear thee, to testify for me.
Foundations of the earth — The mountains properly so called; the sin of Israel is so notorious, that the whole creation may be summoned as a witness against them.
What have I done — What injustice or unkindness? What grievous, burdensome impositions have I laid upon thee. Wearied thee - Speak, what it is hath caused thee to be weary of me?
And Miriam — A prophetess to be assistant to her brothers, and to be an example and a counsellor to the women.

Shittim — This is the place where Balak began by the women of Midian to debauch Israel as Baalim had counselled, and so continued to do, even to Gilgal, all along the borders of his dominion. The righteousness - His mercy, justice and veracity.
Wherewith — One whose heart was touched by the preceeding expostulation, may be supposed to make this enquiry.
Thousands — Ever so many. Ten thousands of rivers - Were it possible to give them.

He — God hath already told you in his word, with what you ought to come before him. To do justly - To render to every one their due, superiors, equals, inferiors, to be equal to all, and oppress none, in body, goods or name; in all your dealings with men carry a chancery in your own beasts, and do according to equity. To love mercy - To be kind, merciful and compassionate to all, not using severity towards any. Walk humbly with thy God - Keep up a constant fellowship with God, by humble, holy faith.
Who — Who shall so dwell in thy church here, as to dwell with thee forever in heaven?

Uprightly — Loving, and serving God, and loving his neighbour not in word only, but in truth; and this constantly. Worketh - Makes it his business to do justly, to give to every one his due, first to God, and then to men. Speaketh - His words and professions to God and men, agree with the thoughts and purposes of his heart.

He — He that doth not speak evil of his neighbour. neighbour - That is, any man. Nor taketh - Into his mouth, doth not raise it, neither spread or propagate it; or believe it without sufficient reason.

Vile — An ungodly man. honoureth - He highly esteems and loves them, though they be mean as to their worldly condition, and though they may differ from him in some opinions or practices of lesser moment. Sweareth - A promissory oath. Hurt - To his own damage. As if a man solemnly swear, that he will sell him such an estate at a price below the full worth; or that, he will give a poor man such a sum of money, which afterwards he finds inconvenient to him. Changeth not - His purpose, but continues firm and resolved to perform his promise.

To usury — In such a manner as is contrary to God's law: of which see otherwise, Exod. xxii, 25 Levit xxv, 36, 37, &c. Reward - Or, a bribe for him who hath a bad cause. Moved - He shall abide with God here, and when he dies be forever with the Lord. David professes his trust in God, his adherence to him and love of his people, ver. 1-3. His satisfaction in God, ver. 4-7. He speaks in the person of Christ, of Gods presence with him, of his resurrection and the glory that should follow, ver. 8-11. Michtam of David. Title of the psalm. Michtam - This seems to be a title belonging to the musick or the song, which, with the rest, is now lost and unknown. As David was both a member, and an eminent type, of Christ, he speaks of himself sometimes in the one and sometimes in the other capacity: and therefore having spoken of himself as a member of Christ, in the former part of the psalm, he proceeds to consider himself as a type of Christ, and being inspired by the holy Ghost: towards the close he speaks such things, as though they might be accommodated to himself in a very imperfect sense, yet could not properly, belong to any but to Christ, to whom therefore they are justly appropriated in the New Testament.

glossa.text: *He that. ((Ibid.))* The answer of the Lord, etc. *as far as* as Christ the lamb, without breaking of members, who properly entered the temple, not that he might be expiated like the rest, but without stain. *He worketh justice.* As when he cast out of the temple those that sold and bought.

*He that speaketh.* Here he follows it out more fully. Truth is when the thing is so as it is said: this Christ did properly. *In his heart,* who at times kept silence toward the unworthy who questioned him fraudulently. *He hath not wrought deceit.* Deceit is in the tongue, when one thing is said and another is in the breast. Or, *he hath not wrought deceit,* because all that he heard from the Father, without any addition or suppression, he made known to his neighbours, that is, to the disciples; to the Jews, his neighbours according to the flesh. *Nor hath he done evil to his neighbour.* But he prayed for them; he did not take up reproach against his neighbours, as is plain from this, that he did not tear Judas with a biting rebuke.

*To nothing,* etc. ((AUG.)) This is perfection, that the malignant one avail nothing in a man, and that this be in his sight, that is, that he know for certain that no one is malignant save he who turns from the Creator to created things. *The malignant one,* that is, the devil, is despised; as when he said: *Go back, Satan,* etc. On the contrary, *he glorifieth them that fear the Lord.* He swore, when he promised the apostles with most certain truth: *Now I will not call you servants, but friends.*

*He that sweareth to his neighbour,* etc. ((Ibid.)) These three things are not great, etc., *as far as* since in the conclusion above he set down a past tense, *he is brought to nothing.*

*Money.* Either it is earthly, which is utterly forbidden to be given out at usury, and which the Lord handed over to Judas to be paid out to the poor, not for usury. Or it is spiritual, which is commanded to be given out at usury, that is, preaching for the instructing of men. *And gifts against the innocent.* Christ does indeed receive gifts, as from the Magi, and daily devout offerings; but not against the innocent; rather he gave his soul for them. *He that doeth these things shall not be moved.* Behold the complete answer to the questioner: he does them (he says), that he may invite us to the act, not only to the singing of them. *He that doeth these things shall not be moved.* ((CASS.)) The conclusion. In like manner he that doeth these things shall rest on the mountain.

notes.text: To them that perish — By obstinately rejecting the only name whereby they can be saved. But to us who are saved - Now saved from our sins, and in the way to everlasting salvation, it is the great instrument of the power of God.
For it is written — And the words are remarkably applicable to this great event. Isaiah xxix, 14

Where is the wise? &c. — The deliverance of Judea from Sennacherib is what Isaiah refers to in these words; in a bold and beautiful allusion to which, the apostle in the clause that follows triumphs over all the opposition of human wisdom to the victorious gospel of Christ. What could the wise men of the gentiles do against this? or the Jewish scribes? or the disputers of this world? - Those among both, who, proud of their acuteness, were fond of controversy, and thought they could confute all opponents. Hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world - That is, shown it to be very foolishness. Isaiah xxxiii, 18

For since in the wisdom of God — According to his wise disposals, leaving them to make the trial. The world - Whether Jewish or gentile, by all its boasted wisdom knew not God - Though the whole creation declared its Creator, and though he declared himself by all the prophets; it pleased God, by a way which those who perish count mere foolishness, to save them that believe.

For whereas the Jews demand of the apostles, as they did of their Lord, more signs still, after all they have seen already; and the Greeks, or gentiles, seek wisdom — The depths of philosophy, and the charms of eloquence.

We go on to preach, in a plain and historical, not rhetorical or philosophical, manner, Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumblingblock — Just opposite to the "signs" they demand. And to the Greeks foolishness - A silly tale, just opposite to the wisdom they seek.

But to them that are called — And obey the heavenly calling. Christ - With his cross, his death, his life, his kingdom. And they experience, first, that he is the power, then, that he is the wisdom, of God.
Because the foolishness of God — The gospel scheme, which the world judge to be mere foolishness, is wiser than the wisdom of men; and, weak as they account it, stronger than all the strength of men.
Behold your calling — What manner of men they are whom God calls. That not many wise men after the flesh - In the account of the world. Not many mighty - Men of power and authority.
Things that are not — The Jews frequently called the gentiles, "Them that are not," 2 Esdras vi. 56, 57. In so supreme contempt did they hold them. The things that are - In high esteem.
That no flesh — A fit appellation. Flesh is fair, but withering as grass. May glory before God - In God we ought to glory.

Of him — Out of his free grace and mercy. Are ye Engrafted into Christ Jesus, who is made unto us that believe wisdom, who were before utterly foolish and ignorant. Righteousness - The sole ground of our justification, who were before under the wrath and curse of God. Sanctification - A principle of universal holiness, whereas before we were altogether dead in sin. And redemption - That is, complete deliverance from all evil, and eternal bliss both of soul and body.
Let him glory in the Lord — Not in himself, not in the flesh, not in the world. Jer. ix, 23, 24

glossa.text:
*To them that perish.* That is, to the wise men of the world, whose wisdom both perishes and is shown to be false, and who themselves are to be damned.

*The power of God.* In that, being slain, he conquered the devil and set man free, or he gives power to believers, by which miracles are done, when the matter requires.

*For it is written.* Therefore he did not send me in wisdom, because he had foretold that he would not receive it into the preaching of the gospel, but would destroy it and reject it from the college of his preachers: and so it was done.

*It pleased God, by the foolishness of preaching, to save them that believe.* That is, that by the faith of the cross eternity should come to mortals: that salvation might be found there, where foolishness is believed.

*For see.* Truly the foolish and weak thing of God is wiser and stronger than men. Which you can prove in yourselves. For unwise and weak men called you, among the foolish and weak things of God such callers are numbered, who nevertheless confound the wise and the strong. And truly they are such, *for there are not many wise.* But he does not say, *none,* perhaps on his own account, who alone among the apostles was skilled in secular letters, rich in earthly goods, and conspicuous by kindred of Roman rank; who nevertheless counted these things as nothing, and did not use them.

*But the foolish things.* Behold, they act openly against the ordinance of God, because they boast the wisdom of the world, while God sets forth humility. For God came humble, seeking the humble, not the lofty. And although he first chose the poor, the unlearned, the weak, yet he does not leave the wise, the rich, the noble, but if he were to choose these first, they would seem to themselves to be chosen for the merit of such things; and so there would be in them the pride by which man fell. Unless the fisherman had gone faithfully before, the humble orator would not have followed. Whence Nathanael, a learned man, was not chosen for an apostle.
*That no flesh may glory.* Of itself, but of God, which is shown there: he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord.
*But of him.* Let no one glory of himself, but yet there is another glory, because of him you are.

notes.text: And seeing the multitudes — At some distance, as they were coming to him from every quarter. He went up into the mountain - Which was near: where there was room for them all. His disciples - not only his twelve disciples, but all who desired to learn of him.

And he opened his mouth — A phrase which always denotes a set and solemn discourse; and taught them - To bless men; to make men happy, was the great business for which our Lord came into the world. And accordingly he here pronounces eight blessings together, annexing them to so many steps in Christianity. Knowing that happiness is our common aim, and that an innate instinct continually urges us to the pursuit of it, he in the kindest manner applies to that instinct, and directs it to its proper object. Though all men desire, yet few attain, happiness, because they seek it where it is not to be found. Our Lord therefore begins his Divine institution, which is the complete art of happiness, by laying down before all that have ears to hear, the true and only true method of acquiring it. Observe the benevolent condescension of our Lord. He seems, as it were, to lay aside his supreme authority as our legislator, that he may the better act the part of: our friend and saviour. Instead of using the lofty style, in positive commands, he, in a more gentle and engaging way, insinuates his will and our duty, by pronouncing those happy who comply with it.

Happy are the poor — In the following discourse there is,

1. A sweet invitation to true holiness and happiness, ver. 3-12.

2. A persuasive to impart it to others, ver. 13-16.

3. A description of true Christian holiness, ver. 17; chap.vii, 12. (in which it is easy to observe, the latter part exactly answers the former.)

4. The conclusion: giving a sure mark of the true way, warning against false prophets, exhorting to follow after holiness. The poor in spirit - They who are unfeignedly penitent, they who are truly convinced of sin; who see and feel the state they are in by nature, being deeply sensible of their sinfulness, guiltiness, helplessness. For theirs is the kingdom of heaven - The present inward kingdom: righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost, as well as the eternal kingdom, if they endure to the end. Luke vi, 20.

They that mourn — Either for their own sins, or for other men's, and are steadily and habitually serious. They shall be comforted - More solidly and deeply even in this world, and eternally in heaven.

Happy are the meek — They that hold all their passions and affections evenly balanced. They shall inherit the earth - They shall have all things really necessary for life and godliness. They shall enjoy whatever portion God hath given them here, and shall hereafter possess the new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness.
They that hunger and thirst after righteousness — After the holiness here described. They shall be satisfied with it.

The merciful — The tender-hearted: they who love all men as themselves: They shall obtain mercy - Whatever mercy therefore we desire from God, the same let us show to our brethren. He will repay us a thousand fold, the love we bear to any for his sake.
The pure in heart — The sanctified: they who love God with all their hearts. They shall see God - In all things here; hereafter in glory.

The peace makers — They that out of love to God and man do all possible good to all men. Peace in the Scripture sense implies all blessings temporal and eternal. They shall be called the children of God - Shall be acknowledged such by God and man. One would imagine a person of this amiable temper and behaviour would be the darling of mankind. But our Lord well knew it would not be so, as long as Satan was the prince of this world. He therefore warns them before of the treatment all were to expect, who were determined thus to tread in his steps, by immediately subjoining, Happy are they who are persecuted for righteousness' sake. Through this whole discourse we cannot but observe the most exact method which can possibly be conceived. Every paragraph, every sentence, is closely connected both with that which precedes, and that which follows it. And is not this the pattern for every Christian preacher? If any then are able to follow it without any premeditation, well: if not, let them not dare to preach without it. No rhapsody, no incoherency, whether the things spoken be true or false, comes of the Spirit of Christ.

For righteousness' sake — That is, because they have, or follow after, the righteousness here described. He that is truly a righteous man, he that mourns, and he that is pure in heart, yea, all that will live godly in Christ Jesus, shall suffer persecution, 2 Tim. iii, 12. The world will always say, Away with such fellows from the earth. They are made to reprove our thoughts. They are grievous to us even to behold. Their lives are not like other men's; their ways are of another fashion.
Revile — When present: say all evil - When you are absent.
Your reward — Even over and above the happiness that naturally and directly results from holiness.

glossa.text:
*And Jesus seeing. ((AUG.))* With this Luke agrees, saying: *And it came to pass in those days, he went out into a mountain to pray ((Luc. VI))*, etc. But Luke says, etc., *as far as* for not all men can do all things: which is thought the truer, although the same [sermon] of both may be seen to have been delivered at once.

*He went up.* Teaching his own to go up and not to remain in the crowd: being about to teach a higher righteousness than that which is of the Scribes and the Pharisees. He himself, a mountain, went up into a mountain, that he might teach the higher summits of the virtues, and might show that the Church, above which he sits preaching, is to be raised more loftily by the Lord's precept, which the same teaching would more fully instruct unto the end of the world. He leads the apostles apart more eminently, that from the mountain the mountains may first receive peace for the people. *He was set down.* The sitting is of the humanity, by which he is known. Whence: *And the world knew him not,* before the incarnation. *They came.* That they may hear the nearer, who hasten in mind to fulfil.

*And opening.* The opening of the mouth signifies the depth of the sacrament. He opened as it were an abyss, as it were a treasure, as it were a river of paradise. On this mountain he writes the New Testament in the hearts of sons, beginning from beatitude, who on mount Sinai gave the Old Testament on stones to servants, beginning from terror.

((AUG.)) The sermon which our Lord spoke on the mountain, as in the Gospel, etc., *as far as, Everyone who hears these my words and shall do them, I will liken him to a wise man ((Matth. VII))*.

*Blessed. ((GREG. NYSS.))* Beatitude, as my opinion carries it, is the comprehension of all those things which, etc., *as far as* for misery is a wretchedness in bitter and sorrowful chances and calamities that do not fall out by our own will.

*Blessed are the poor.* The number of the sentences is to be diligently attended to. For beatitude begins from humility.

*((HIER.)) Blessed are the poor in spirit.* Because it is not necessity but faith, and the devotion of poverty, that makes men blessed, etc., *as far as* as the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, so poverty is the beginning of beatitude.

((CHRYSOST.)) The poor in spirit are the humble and contrite of heart. And by spirit he here means the soul and the will. But because many are humble not of their own accord, but constrained by necessity, he calls the first sort blessed.

*Blessed are the meek.* The meek are those who master evil habits: perfect virtue is the possession of one's habits.

 ((THEOPH.)) The meek are not those who are not angry at all, etc., *as far as* so the doctrine of a man is discerned through patience.

*They shall possess the land. ((AUG.))* That land I believe to be the one of which it is said in the Psalm: *Thou art my hope, my portion in the land of the living ((Psal. CLXI))*.

*Blessed are they that mourn.* For their own sins or for others', which mourning is from the lower watering, but that which comes from the upper watering is out of desire for the heavenly country. The one washes present filth, the other kindles more sharply the lovers of eternal things. But he who has laid down his sins, has corrected his habits by meekness, and has wept besides, can now hunger and thirst after righteousness, which before he could not. This virtue is not fulfilled without the spirit of fortitude: because through him, by hungering, we shall one day come to fulness. *Blessed are they that mourn.* It remains, after the things aforesaid, to purge by mourning the foulness of our ruins. Mourning for sins or out of heavenly desire earns consolation, and no other does.

These are enlightened by the spirit of knowledge, that they may know in what evils they are wrapped.

((HILAR.)) For those that mourn, not for those grieving over bereavements, or insults, or losses, but for those weeping over their old sins, and made wretched by the consciousness of the crimes with which we are befouled, this assiduous consolation is prepared in heaven.

*Blessed are they that hunger.* Lovers of the good word, to whom it is not enough that they are just, but they always thirst for the work of righteousness.

Righteousness is to render to each his own, to oneself, and to one's neighbors, and to God. This righteousness will not be fully fulfilled until God be all in all: therefore here we can hunger, not be filled. The light of righteousness is mercy, the strength of mercy is righteousness; this mercy has need of the spirit of counsel, without which no one is merciful with circumspection. The beginning is to have mercy on oneself, the end is to die for another. For the order of showing mercy is that each man begin from himself. Christ hints at the end, having died out of mercy for sinners.

*Blessed are the merciful.* Mercy is born of the things that go before, because if true humility has gone before, and the mind grows meek, and weeps for its own falls and others', and hungers after righteousness, afterwards true mercy is born. For then it will make others' miseries its own and will help according to its powers: and if the means of helping is wanting, compassion will not be wanting: *Be ye merciful as your Father also is merciful ((Luc. VI))*, that is, let us have mercy unto that end unto which God also has mercy, that goodness may overflow upon all: mercy without righteousness is called remission and lukewarmness; righteousness without mercy is called severity and harshness.

*Blessed are the peacemakers. ((RAB.))* The peacemakers are those who compose all the motions of the mind and subject them to reason, because nothing resists those who are like the Father, etc., *as far as* but when God shall be all in all, then the beatitude of adoption will be given.

*Blessed are they that suffer persecution.* In the seven aforesaid there is the showing and the proving of perfection. Those who have the aforesaid things can suffer persecution: and he rightly holds the aforesaid things which he has received who is ready to die for them.

*Blessed are you when they shall revile you.* Thus far he set down his sentences generally, as though to those absent, although they belonged to those present also, now he turns his words to them (although this belongs to others also), foretelling how great things they should suffer for his name: because he wished to make known to them the dignity of their rank, saying: *You are the salt of the earth, you are the light of the world;* that from the sad things they might take humility, from the glad things consolation.

*Shall revile.* The ancient translation has: *When men shall hate you, and shall say all that is evil, and shall cast you out.* Yet the sense is the same in ours, since revilings come from hatred of the heart. He who chooses the glory of heaven does not fear reproach on earth; as much as each man rejoices at the praise of men, so much does he grieve at reproach. Him whom praise lifts up, blame casts down: where a man seeks to be praised only before God, he does not fear to be confounded in the sight of men. *Lying.* He adds this, lest he glory of whom evil things are truly said. He adds also: *For my sake,* because sometimes false things are said, which comes about through the rashness of men, yet they do not suffer this for Christ's sake, whom they do not follow.

*For your reward is very great in heaven.* Not in rolling things, since an eternal reward ought not to be in rolling things, but in spiritual firmaments, where everlasting righteousness dwells. Already therefore they feel this reward who rejoice in spiritual goods. But it will be made perfect when this mortal shall put on immortality. *For so they persecuted,* etc. He tempers the rigor of the passion by an example. Persecution is made in three ways: by hatred of the heart, by words, by deeds.

registers.label: Spare
lines: What does the Lord require of you?
To do justice, and to love kindness.
Blessed are the poor, the mourning, the meek.
Theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
God has shown you what is good.
And to walk humbly with our God.
Come, let us worship the God of the lowly.
We come to walk humbly. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: God has a case to make this morning, and it is not a hard riddle: he has already told you what is good.
To do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly with our God.
Not rivers of oil, not grand offerings, not the proud and the strong the world counts on — God chose the weak things instead.
To do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly with our God.
And on the mountain Jesus turns the blessing toward the ones we overlook: the poor, the grieving, the gentle, the hungry for right.
To do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly with our God.
So come down off your high places, friends, and walk the low road home with your God.
To do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly with our God. Amen.
